paper_title: SEEK: Self-Evolution through Execution Knowledge for Agentic Robot Manipulation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: General-purpose multimodal foundation models enable robots to adapt during deployment from observations and execution feedback, without task-specific demonstrations or training. However, the robot retains what it learns only in the model's working context. Once the task ends, it loses this execution knowledge, such as how to carry a bowl between two grippers. On the next attempt at the task, the robot may take just as long and repeat the same mistakes. To avoid this repetition, robots must retain execution knowledge across attempts. Yet replaying past actions is insufficient, because their effects depend on the current conditions. Procedures that determine actions from the current scene address this, but when they meet conditions that earlier attempts did not cover, revising them requires the measured effects of earlier actions. We therefore propose SEEK, an agentic framework that retains both, enabling robots to improve across attempts while keeping the underlying model fixed. To adapt retained knowledge to the current scene, SEEK adopts a Self-Evolving Programmatic Policy (SEPP) that encodes manipulation as executable procedures and determines each action from current observations. As the robot executes these procedures, SEEK records the measured effects of its actions, including those from failed attempts, in a Persistent Action-Effect Bank (PAEB). Where a retained procedure applies, it acts without a model request; where it meets a condition it does not cover, this evidence guides its revision. On RoboDojo, knowledge retained over ten attempts raises SEEK's average task score from 27.0 to 54.4 and its success rate from 19.7% to 48.0% across all 42 tasks. On 34 of these tasks with GPT-6.2 Astra, SEEK reaches 80.1 after five attempts, against 49.6 for the same model acting directly, and uses 77.6% fewer model requests. https://zeyangguan.github.io/SEEK-Agentic-Robot-Manipulation/

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: General-purpose multimodal foundation models enable robots to adapt during deployment from observations and execution feedback, without task-specific demonstrations or training. However, the robot retains what it learns only in the models working context. Once the task ends, it loses this execution knowledge, such as how to carry bowl between two grippers. On the next attempt at the task, the robot may take just as long and repeat the same mistakes. To avoid this repetition, robots must retain execution knowledge across attempts. Yet replaying past actions is insufficient, because their effects depend on the current conditions. Procedures that determine actions from the current scene address this, but when they meet conditions that earlier attempts did not cover, revising them requires the measured effects of earlier actions. We therefore propose SEEK, an agentic framework that retains both, enabling robots to improve across attempts while keeping the underlying model fixed. To adapt retained knowledge to the current scene, SEEK adopts Self-Evolving Programmatic Policy (SEPP) that encodes manipulation as executable procedures and determines each action from current observations. As the robot executes these procedures, SEEK records the measured effects of its actions, including those from failed attempts, in Persistent Action-Effect Bank (PAEB). Where retained procedure applies, it acts without model request; where it meets condition it does not cover, this evidence guides its revision. On RoboDojo, knowledge retained over ten attempts raises SEEKs average task score from 27.0 to 54.4 and its success rate from 19.7% to 48.0% across all 42 tasks. On 34 of these tasks with GPT-6.2 Astra, SEEK reaches 80.1 after five attempts, against 49.6 for the same model acting directly, and uses 77.6% fewer model requests. 1. Introduction Recent advances in robot learning have been driven by scaling demonstration data and model capacity, producing policies with broader task coverage and stronger generalization [4, 10, 20, 27, 28, 40]. Yet these capabilities remain bounded by the distributions represented in the training data [4, 13, 20]. Extending these policies to new embodiments, tasks, or conditions beyond this coverage typically requires additional data collection, training, or fine-tuning [1, 9, 10, 18, 20]. As result, capability growth remains closely coupled to pre-collected demonstrations and the imitation distribution they define [13, 28]. 1 Figure 1. Motivation and central idea of SEEK. Top: GPT-6 Astra [29] acting directly keeps what the robot learns only in its working context and loses it once the task ends, so the next attempt may repeat the same mistakes; on real robot, the last cube of square is again grasped and set down, leaving gap. Bottom: SEEK retains this execution knowledge across attempts as action-effect evidence (PAEB), including that of failed attempts, and reusable procedures (SEPP), while the model remains fixed; its next attempt pushes the cube in. Right: with GPT-6.2 Astra on 34 RoboDojo tasks, task score by category and model requests per episode of SEEK after 5 attempts and of the model acting directly [38]. General-purpose multimodal models offer another route to robot adaptation through reasoning during deployment [14, 16, 17, 22]. By combining current visual observations with task instructions and execution feedback, these models can guide the robots actions and adjust its behavior as execution unfolds [14, 15, 24]. Through this interaction, the robot acquires execution knowledge: the effects its actions produce under given conditions and the procedures that prove effective. For example, it may find that thin coin remains on the table when pinched at its center but lifts when pinched at its rim. However, the robot retains this knowledge only within the models working context. Once the task ends, the knowledge is lost. On its next attempt, the robot may again pinch the coin at its center before rediscovering the rim, taking just as long as before. Avoiding this repetition requires retaining execution knowledge across attempts. Yet simply replaying past actions is insufficient. The same action can yield different effects under different conditions. The robot therefore needs reusable procedures that determine each action from the current scene. Existing and concurrent approaches have begun to retain such procedures as skills and programs [13, 21, 23, 33, 34]. However, retaining procedure does not ensure that it will handle conditions beyond those encountered in earlier attempts. When procedure encounters such conditions, measured action effects provide evidence for deciding how to revise it. This evidence should include actions from failed attempts. Procedures and measured action effects therefore need to be retained together, so that procedure can act without the model where it applies and be revised from this evidence where it does not. Existing methods that keep action-level evidence still leave each action to the model or learned policy [23, 35, 36], while programs that act without the model are frozen once developed [12]. To this end, we introduce SEEK, framework for agentic robot manipulation that enables self-evolution through execution knowledge while keeping the underlying model fixed. SEEK retains this knowledge in two coupled forms. At the procedure level, Self-Evolving Programmatic Policy (SEPP) encodes observation, action generation, verification, task progression, and recovery as executable procedures. During execution, these procedures use current observations to determine actions. At the action level, Persistent Action-Effect 2 Bank (PAEB) records the measured effect of each executed action with its execution context, including actions from failed attempts. Drawing on these records, the fixed model makes decisions or revises procedure, and each revision retains references to its supporting evidence. Together, the two components form continual self-improvement loop: execution supplies evidence for policy revision, and revised procedures carry the resulting capability into subsequent attempts. Once retained procedure applies to the current scene, it can generate actions without another model request, so successive attempts reuse previously acquired behavior instead of repeating model deliberation. We evaluate SEEK on RoboDojo [6], simulation benchmark of 42 dual-arm manipulation tasks. To isolate the contribution of retained knowledge, we compare the same system with and without it on scenes unseen during self-evolution; both conditions allow adaptation within an attempt. Across the 42 tasks, knowledge retained over ten attempts more than doubles task performance. Compared with GPT-6.2 Astra acting directly on 34 of these tasks, SEEK with the same model raises the task score from 49.6 to 80.1 after five attempts and uses 77.6% fewer model requests. We further measure the fraction of executed steps generated by retained procedures, and ablate PAEB and SEPP to separate the contributions of action-level evidence reuse and procedure-level policy evolution. Finally, on smaller set of tasks, we replace the underlying model and run SEEK on real robot; in both settings, SEEK again improves task performance. Contributions. We explore self-evolution through execution knowledge and introduce SEEK, which comprises PAEB, recording the measured effect of each executed action, and SEPP, an executable policy revised from these records. On RoboDojo, SEEK reaches an average task score of 54.4 (+27.4) and success rate of 48.0% (+28.3) across all 42 tasks, compared with 27.0 and 19.7% for the same system without retained knowledge. With GPT-6.2 Astra, SEEK reaches 80.1 (+30.5) and 75.0% (+34.3) on 34 of these tasks after five attempts, compared with 49.6 and 40.7% for the same model acting directly. 2. Related Work Foundation Models for Robot Control. Foundation models support robot control through learned action policies [20, 40] and agents that reason during execution [15, 17]. General-purpose multimodal models can also act as the policy directly, deciding each action from observations and execution feedback without task-specific demonstrations or training [38]. The execution knowledge such an agent gains is held only in the models working context and is lost once the task ends. Reusable Programs for Robot Manipulation. Executable programs preserve control logic as reusable procedures. Code as Policies and ProgPrompt express robot behavior as programs that compose available perception and action interfaces [22, 32]. PyRUA-Lean extends these interfaces with Python cells that perform local checks, retries, and selective observation without additional model requests [31]. These cells build on primitive library that its authors wrote for the benchmarks dual-arm station and on operating notes, including how strictly the benchmark judges final scene. Its programs are written anew in each attempt, which therefore starts from what the authors supplied rather than from what earlier attempts revealed. retained program that acts without the model removes repeated deliberation for behavior already resolved, and one that also remains revisable during execution can be corrected as soon as it meets condition that earlier attempts did not cover. COAP retains its programs. Coding agents develop shared library for perception, state tracking, and control through offline refinement from execution traces, then freeze the code for execution without the model [12]. This refinement uses state information that robot acting from its own observations does not have. The agents compare the measured object state against simulator ground truth, and the perception code takes the object shapes published with the benchmark as constants. Once frozen, the code can no longer 3 Table 1. Capabilities for cumulative self-improvement. Header colors mark adaptivity within an attempt, memory across attempts, and autonomy . Online revision adapts ongoing execution; self-acquired knowledge marks methods whose knowledge comes from their own attempts rather than from demonstrations, ground-truth object states from the simulator, or knowledge written by their authors for the benchmark; effect evidence preserves actionoutcome records; self-executing procedures are retained procedures that generate actions without model request where they apply; and executable reuse retains acquired procedures. Method Online revision Self-acquired knowledge Effect evidence Self-executing procedures Executable reuse RoboICL [24] PyRUA-Lean [31] LEXP [36] RoboDoctor [35] EmbodiedEvo [21] HexaShell [8] RoboFoundry [23] COAP [12] SEEK (ours) be revised when it meets condition that development did not cover, such as an object below fixed size threshold, and each new task requires further offline development. Voyager, PhysicalRSI, and RoboFoundry keep their skills revisable from execution [23, 26, 34], but the model remains in the loop; in RoboFoundry it is called at every step. Retained Experience for Robot Manipulation. Interaction history, lessons, and execution evidence preserve what prior actions have revealed. Reflexion and ExpeL retain reflections and extracted insights, while DROC distills language corrections into reusable knowledge [30, 37, 39]. RoboICL conditions the model on task demonstration and keeps observations, actions, and execution receipts only within an attempt [24]. LEXP and RoboDoctor carry lessons and execution records across attempts together with their supporting evidence [35, 36], but as context for the model. Neither retains an executable procedure, so each action is still decided by the model or by the learned policy it supervises. EmbodiedEvo brings procedural and diagnostic knowledge together by distilling physical feedback into reusable code Skills and Lessons during exploration in separate scene [21]. Only these distilled artifacts reach the test scene, where they are read-only. The interaction records behind them are not carried over, and the coding agent still writes each program that calls the Skills. HexaShell develops its tools on the task itself. After each development attempt, an optimizer agent reads the attempts log and adds or repairs task-specific tools, which are then frozen [8]. As with EmbodiedEvo, what carries forward is the distilled tools and notes rather than the records, and the acting agent still issues every command that calls tool. SEEK couples persistent action-effect evidence with revisable executable procedures, both acquired from the robots own attempts, allowing observed effects to directly support procedure revision and subsequent execution. Where retained procedure applies, it generates actions without model request; where it meets condition it does not cover, the fixed model revises it within the attempt. Table 1 compares these capabilities. 3. Method 3.1. Problem Setting We consider repeated attempts at manipulation task specified by language instruction, where an attempt is one execution of the task from an initial scene layout until success or the step limit. Attempts that update this knowledge are evolution attempts. The initial knowledge K0 contains no task-specific evidence or procedures, and execution initially relies on the models action candidates. 3.2. Overview As shown in Fig. 2, our proposed SEEK retains execution knowledge in two coupled forms: K𝑘 = {E𝑘, Π𝑘 }, (2) where E𝑘 contains the measured effects of executed actions and their execution context in PAEB, while Π𝑘 encodes executable procedures in SEPP. During an attempt, these procedures use the current observations to determine actions and check progress. Then, each executed action adds evidence to PAEB, regardless of whether it produces the expected effect. 5 When procedure requests help or execution stalls, the model checks the current observations and retrieved evidence to guide the execution or revision of the procedure. After the attempt, the model reviews the trace and outcome to select the procedures to retain. The next attempt reuses these procedures and accumulated evidence, while initializing scene-dependent state from its own observations (Sec. 3.5). 3.3. Self-Evolving Programmatic Policy In order to reuse procedure across scene layouts, its actions must be determined based on current observations rather than fixed by previous executions. To this end, we design the Self-Evolving Programmatic Policy (SEPP), which organizes these procedures into main program that controls task progression and reusable operations that execute behaviors: Π𝑘 = (𝑃𝑘, O𝑘), (3) where 𝑃𝑘 is the main program and O𝑘 contains named operations. The main program and each operation are procedures, each defining decision routine and optionally an observation routine, which updates the local state and evaluates the effects. The main program calls operations using scene-dependent parameters, and an operation can select another operation or return control to the main program. To execute in the current scene, these procedures derive operation parameters and local targets from the current observations. They access RGB images, camera calibration, and robot proprioception through shared executable interface. The fixed model binds task-relevant object or part as named role by giving camera, box in the current image, and optionally text concept. SAM3 [5] segments the instance in the box, and its temporal memory propagates the mask to later images of that camera without further model requests. When the track is lost, the role is located again by matching its reference crop, confirmed by forwardbackward optical flow and new segmentation; otherwise, the role is marked invalid. Metric estimates are computed only when procedure requests them. An image point per camera is triangulated from two or three calibrated cameras, or single ray is intersected with supplied plane height, and the estimate is returned with its ray residual and reprojection errors, so the procedure can test whether correspondence is geometrically consistent. Silhouette-based estimates fit shape hypothesis to the masks of one to three views under supplied support height. End-effector poses and gripper measurements come from robot state. For example, the distance to 𝑔𝑡 in Fig. 2 compares the observed end-effector position with specified target. An unavailable or invalid measurement is recorded as missing and never filled in from command or an earlier step, so an objective that depends on it cannot be completed by assumption, and perception errors remain separable from action errors in the records. The interface also provides motion-feasibility queries and dispatches end-effector and gripper commands under motion constraints. At decision step 𝑡, the active procedure incorporates the current observation and determines the next action 𝑎𝑡 . When numerical objective is used, 𝑔𝑡 specifies target features, tolerances, and applicability conditions. The procedure can generate an action from current measurements or select still-valid candidate supplied by the fixed model. After dispatch, an execution receipt records the command actually executed and the robot states before and after it. The same operation and objective may span several such steps. fixed progress monitor, separate from the revisable policy, requests model review after sustained lack of motion, oscillation, or weak response to commands. Execution reveals which part of procedure needs to change: target derivation, motion generation, effect assessment, operation composition, or recovery. The fixed model uses current observations and retrieved PAEB records to revise the main program, given as complete source, or selected operations, given as complete source or as literal edits against an identified stored version. If any check fails, nothing is installed and the error is returned with the next request; otherwise, bindings, versions, objective, and candidates are installed together, and the revised policy chooses the next action on the same observation. Procedures are written in restricted subset of Python without imports, classes, exception handling, or file and network access, are bounded in size, run time, and call depth, and reach the robot only through the executable interface, so every motion they request passes the same executor as model candidate. An accepted version is identified by the hash of its source and stored with its provenance; versions are therefore never overwritten, and later review can revert harmful one (Sec. 3.5). Updating an operation preserves unrelated procedures; the current invocation keeps its version, and subsequent invocation selects the updated one. The interpreter, measurement interfaces, motion constraints, progress monitor, and the initial routine that delegates decisions to the fixed model remain fixed runtime components; the observation and decision logic built on them can evolve. 3.4. Persistent Action-Effect Bank Once its working context is lost, the fixed model no longer knows which actions have been tried or what each produced, and may repeat an ineffective action without recognizing it. PAEB retains this knowledge outside 7 the model as bank of the measured effects of executed actions, effective and ineffective alike, and supplies the evidence for revising procedures. For each executed action within an attempt, it records transition 𝑒𝑡 = (𝑥𝑡 , 𝑎𝑡 , 𝑥𝑡+1, 𝑐𝑡 , ℓ𝑡 ), (4) where 𝑥𝑡 and 𝑥𝑡+1 contain observations and measured state before and after execution, 𝑎𝑡 is the dispatched action, and 𝑐𝑡 records its execution context. The provenance ℓ𝑡 links the record to its attempt, procedure version, operation invocation, and execution receipt. multi-step operation is represented by its invocation and linked transitions, so the interval illustrated in Fig. 2 summarizes an execution segment. Model proposals, errors, effect assessments, and reviews retain their own record types and sources. Evidence from failed attempts remains available for diagnosing ineffective actions and recovering useful partial procedures. Given request 𝑞𝑡 from the fixed model or procedure, PAEB returns R𝑡 = Recall(E, 𝑞𝑡 ), (5) where is the currently available bank, comprising E𝑘1 and the records of the current attempt. Revising procedure requires the records behind it, which show what each action produced in the context where it was executed. record that only resembles the current situation may stem from different condition and mislead the revision, so Recall selects records by reference rather than by resemblance. Records refer to one another by IDs that encode the attempt and the step, and each version of the main program or an operation stores the IDs of the records cited when it was written, so the evidence behind revision stays attached to it. Source-attempt and record-type filters first fix the eligible records; request that matches nothing returns an empty result rather than records of other attempts or types. Requested IDs then select exact evidence within this scope, and transition also carries the IDs of its observations before and after the action, so citing an observation retrieves the records made at it. textual query, the entry point for records whose IDs are not yet known, ranks the remaining eligible records by the number of distinct tokens they share with it, with ties broken toward the most recent record. Requested IDs that are unknown, filtered out, or beyond the result limit are reported separately, so the model can tell missing evidence from evidence outside its request. The fixed model can then follow the links in the returned records, for example from an operation version to the transitions it cites, and refine its request. request never contains the whole bank. It carries the source of the active procedure, the last 8 transitions and up to 12 earlier ones, the last three reviews, and the current and cited images, while older records appear as references that are resolved on demand, so its size stays bounded as PAEB grows. 3.5. Self-Evolution across Attempts The update in Eq. (1) combines evidence accumulation and policy consolidation. Evidence accumulation is E𝑘 = E𝑘1 ΔE (𝜏𝑘, 𝑦𝑘), (6) where appends execution records and associated assessments and outcomes while preserving earlier evidence. Policy consolidation is Π𝑘 = RevisePolicy(Π𝑘1, 𝜏𝑘, 𝑦𝑘, E𝑘). (7) Starting from the policy as revised online during the attempt, the fixed model reviews the outcome, executed transitions, errors, operation sequences, and available versions. It selects keep, replace, or revert for the main program, and can independently update or restore selected operations. The decision is guided by recurring execution difficulties, contrasting action effects, and the observed use of existing procedures. To support this review, the fixed model can inspect historical observations and replay procedures on recorded inputs. The review does not judge version by the final score alone. Its input groups the transitions by program version 8 and action source, lists errors and model requests by reason, and joins each of the last three reviews with the transitions later executed under the versions it selected, so version is assessed by what happened after it was installed, in this attempt and in later ones. version therefore remains provisional. It is reverted, or its operation restored, when later execution provides evidence against it. The review can also write lessons, textual rules that state when they apply, what to do, what to expect, and what to do if the expectation fails; lessons are included in later requests but are not executed. review is installed only if its code compiles, its references name saved records, and no raw record has changed; otherwise, its validation error is returned for another try, and after three failed tries the previous policy is kept. Attempt 𝑘 + 1 inherits K𝑘, while object bindings, local objectives, operation parameters, and runtime state are initialized from its own observations. still-applicable procedure is executed without further model review, and new challenge provides evidence for further revision. 4. Experiments Our experiments examine whether execution knowledge retained in PAEB and SEPP improves subsequent task performance while the underlying model remains fixed. 4.1. Experimental Setup Benchmark. We evaluate on RoboDojo [6], simulation benchmark of 42 dual-arm manipulation tasks in five capability categories: Generalization, Precision, Long-Horizon, Memory, and Open. The robot observes RGB images from head camera and two wrist cameras together with its proprioceptive state and current camera calibration, and acts through end-effector targets and gripper commands. Depth images and privileged scene-object states are not provided; metric visual estimates use the RGB geometry interfaces of Sec. 3.3. We report the benchmarks task score (0100), which credits partial progress, and its strict success rate (SR), which counts only full-score episodes. Model and Interface. The fixed model is GPT-6 Astra [29] with xhigh reasoning effort. It receives no parameter updates or task demonstrations, and the number of model requests is not capped. All tasks share the same system instructions, tools, and policy initialization. Evolution and Evaluation Protocol. Each task starts from K0 = {E0, Π0}, with no task-specific evidence or procedure. Over 10 evolution attempts on distinct layouts, SEEK updates its knowledge after each attempt by Eq. (1) to obtain K10. The main results evaluate this snapshot over 50 episodes per task on layouts unseen during evolution, together with no-carryover control that starts the same episodes from K0. Each evaluation episode is single attempt that starts from fresh working copy of its designated snapshot, allows feedback, evidence collection, and online revision within the episode, and discards all updates at its end. Generalization tasks use 25 standard and 25 randomized episodes. Unless noted otherwise, SEEK refers to the system with K10. Metrics. Operation reuse is the fraction of executed steps generated by operations in O𝑘 retained from earlier attempts. Model requests are counted per episode, whether for scene interpretation, action candidates, or procedure revisions. Analysis Tasks. For the analyses in Secs. 4.34.4, we randomly select one or two tasks from each category, yielding nine tasks: Stack Bowls, Insert Tubes, Classify Objects, Swap T, Classify Objects by Language, Make Toast, Deposit Coin, Organize Table, and Match and Pick from Conveyor. The last column gives the averages. 4.2. Comparison on RoboDojo Table 2 compares SEEK with learned policies and agent-based methods across all 42 tasks and lists the setting of each method. SEEK reaches an average score of 54.4 and an SR of 48.0%. Among the listed methods, it is highest on the average and in Generalization and Open, level with VPP2 in Precision (43.2 against 43.0), and second in Memory; in Long-Horizon, its score (44.2) is below those of VPP2 (56.3), PhysicalRSI, and InternW0-Δ. SEEK obtains these results from ten attempts per task, without demonstrations or parameter updates, and its margin over the learned policies is largest in Open (63.1 against at most 10.8), the one category for which no demonstrations exist. Table 3 reports scores for 20 representative tasks, four from each category; SEEK attains the highest score on 10 of them. These results compare the capability achieved under each methods protocol, with GPT-6 Astra at medium effort. At the xhigh effort of SEEK, GPT-6 Astra averages 38.5 on ten tasks (five episodes each) [7], against 38.7 for SEEK without carryover and 49.9 with it. GPT-6.2 Astra. We also evaluate SEEK with GPT-6.2 Astra at xhigh effort on the 34 tasks outside Open. For each task, SEEK runs 5 evolution attempts on distinct layouts, and the resulting K5 is evaluated over 10 episodes on unseen layouts under the protocol of Sec. 4.1, with 5 standard and 5 randomized episodes for Generalization tasks. GPT-6.2 Astra acting directly runs the same episodes through the reference harness of RoboProbe [38]. SEEK reaches an average score of 80.1 and an SR of 75.0%, against 49.6 and 40.7% for the direct agent (Table 2 and Fig. 3), and uses 14.1 model requests per episode, against 63.2 (77.6% fewer). 4.3. Cumulative Self-Improvement We compare SEEK with the no-carryover control of Sec. 4.1. Both run the same unseen episodes with the same within-episode adaptation, so their difference measures the contribution of retained knowledge. Across all 42 tasks, retained knowledge raises the average score from 27.0 to 54.4 and the SR from 19.7% to 48.0%  (Table 2)  , with gains in every category and on 37 of the 42 tasks. Evidence collection and online revision within an attempt remain available in every configuration; the configurations differ only in what is carried to the next attempt. Disabling both updates gives the no-carryover control of Sec. 4.3; enabling both gives SEEK with K10. Each of the other two configurations repeats the 10 evolution attempts with one update disabled and is evaluated from its own snapshot after the tenth attempt. In the first case, procedure that meets new condition is revised without the records of earlier attempts; in the second, the model knows what earlier actions produced but must turn this into procedures again in every attempt. With both, SEEK reaches 70.4 and higher score than either alone on every task, so the two components are complementary. Each alone reduces model requests from 54.4 to below 48 per episode; together they reduce them to 41.5. Operation reuse, defined only when procedures are carried, also rises with PAEB carryover, from 68.4% to 82.3% on average. 4.5. Case Study Deposit Coin is Precision task. The robot picks up thin coin lying flat on table and inserts it into piggy bank. Fig. 4 traces the first five attempts, linking PAEB evidence to online revision and post-attempt consolidation in SEPP. Attempt 1 fails, but its PAEB records reveal contrasting effects. center pinch leaves the coin on the table, while rim pinch raises it by 89 mm. Consolidation turns this contrast into rim pinch, SEPP operation that locates the rim in the current observation, approaches with pad offset, and checks the grasp with settle-and-test lift (Fig. 4a, 1). In attempt 3, the fingers settle with joint change below 0.001 mm, yet grasp verification fails. The check requires full closure, which the coin prevents. At step 107, the fixed model revises the check online, citing PAEB records from attempt 1. Verification now requires close command and settled fingers (Fig. 4b, 2). Post-attempt review retains it. Attempt 5 combines both procedures on new layout (Fig. 4c). The first closure misses the coin; the revised check detects the empty test lift, rim pinch re-grasps at the rim, and confirmed lift allows transport and 12 Figure 4. Case study on Deposit Coin. (a) After attempt 1, consolidation creates the rim-pinch operation ( 1) from PAEB evidence. (b) Grasp verification ( 2) is revised online in attempt 3 and retained. (c) Attempt 5 reuses both, with test lift detecting an empty grasp ( 2) and triggering rim re-grasp ( 1). Numbered frames mark the supporting procedure. Orange and purple arrows carry evidence and procedures to later attempts. In each SEPP card, the open tab is the changed operation, with additions in gold and removals dashed. insertion. Relative to attempt 1, grasp acquisition takes 72 steps rather than 281, model requests fall from 63 to 20, and retained operations generate 72% of the executed steps. 4.6. Alternative Model and Real Robot Underlying Model. We test whether self-evolution depends on the fixed model by replacing GPT-6 Astra with Claude Opus 5.5, leaving all other settings unchanged. On three of the analysis tasks, we repeat the 10 evolution attempts and the evaluation on unseen episodes. Retained knowledge raises the average score from 24.0 (K0) to 62.4 (K10) and reduces model requests from 35.7 to 26.0 per episode. Real Robot. We test whether SEEK improves performance under real sensing and actuation by running it on Franka Emika Panda arm. On four tabletop tasks, including Arrange Cubes into Square  (Fig. 1)  , 5 evolution attempts on distinct layouts produce K5, which we evaluate over 10 unseen episodes per task against GPT-6 Astra acting directly at xhigh effort. Relative to this agent, SEEK raises the average score from 66.9 to 83.3 and reduces model requests from 52.2 to 34.4 per episode. Fig. 5 shows the setup and the four tasks. The arm carries Robotiq 2F-140 gripper and uses the system instructions and tools of simulation. As in simulation, it observes RGB images, without depth images or object states, together with its proprioceptive state and camera calibration, and acts through end-effector targets and gripper commands. The images come from two Intel RealSense D435 cameras: wrist camera looking along the fingers and front camera fixed at the far edge of the table, facing the robot. Each episode receives task score from 0 to 100 for the highest level of progress it reaches, and SR counts episodes with full score. An operator scores each episode by the following rules, whose conditions are directly observable; an object is in tray when it lies fully within the trays rim and has been released. Task 1, Put Cube into Tray, puts the red cube into the gray tray, with gray, pink, blue, and yellow trays and red, green, blue, and yellow cubes on the table: 100 if the red cube is in the gray tray and no other object has been placed in any tray, otherwise 0. Task 2, Stack Cubes into Tower, stacks three cubes on coaster in specified order, red at the bottom, then yellow, and blue on top: 20 once the whole bottom face of the red cube rests on the coaster and the cube has been released, 50 once the yellow cube stands stably on it after release, and 100 once the blue cube stands stably on the yellow one and the whole tower stands on its own; the score is 0 if the red cube does not rest on the coaster. Task 3, Sort Items into Trays, puts two fruits into the yellow tray and two cubes into the blue 13 Figure 5. Real-robot setup and tasks. The Franka arm with its wrist and front cameras, and each of the four tasks in an example layout. tray, in any order: 25 for each item that ends in its tray and none for an item in the other tray. Task 4, Arrange Cubes into Square, assembles four cubes into 2 2 square: 100 when all four stand directly on the table, none stacked, and form two complete rows and columns in which adjacent cubes touch, with gap of at most about 5 mm, and are aligned, with rotation difference of at most about 10 and outer faces offset by at most about 5 mm; 60 when the square is incomplete but three cubes, touching and aligned in this way, form an that covers three of its corners; otherwise 0. 5. Conclusion SEEK enables self-evolution across manipulation attempts by coupling measured action-effect evidence with revisable executable procedures. PAEB retains evidence from successful and failed actions; SEPP uses this evidence to refine subsequent execution while the underlying model remains fixed. On RoboDojo, SEEK reaches an average task score of 54.4 and success rate of 48.0% across all 42 tasks, where the knowledge retained over ten attempts more than doubles SEEKs task performance. With GPT-6.2 Astra on 34 of these tasks, SEEK reaches 80.1 after five attempts, against 49.6 for the model acting directly, and uses 77.6% fewer model requests. Limitations. First, although SEEK can revise its main program and operations, its perception tools, executor, and action interface remain fixed, so its performance still depends on these components, including the accuracy of perception models such as SAM3; stronger models could improve perception and support more precise manipulation. Second, our evaluation focuses on dual-arm manipulation in simulation and singlearm manipulation on real Franka arm; extending SEEK to wheeled and humanoid robots would test its generalization to more complex, long-horizon indoor and outdoor tasks. Since knowledge is accumulated separately for each task, we will also study its transfer across tasks and its accumulation over longer periods, including how to compress execution evidence, handle outdated knowledge, and maintain growing procedure library.
